title: Pumping wastewater underground turned Oklahoma into an earthquake hotspot
body: From 1978 to 2008, Oklahoma had about two earthquakes of magnitude 3 or more a year. Then the count soared: 20 in 2009, 109 in 2013 and well over 500 in 2014, when the state recorded more than twice as many earthquakes as California. Researchers link the surge to the water that comes up from oil and gas wells: more than 70% of it is pumped back down into a deep rock layer, the Arbuckle Group, which rests on ancient basement rock, and the rising water pressure in its pores can release the stress on faults. After the strongest quake ever recorded in the state, regulators shut or throttled disposal wells, and in 2017 the shaking dropped sharply.

slides.text: Afterwards the state ordered 37 wastewater disposal wells shut down. As wells closed or cut the volumes they injected, earthquakes fell sharply in 2017.

slides.question: In 2014, how did Oklahoma’s earthquake count compare with California’s?
slides.explanation: Oklahoma recorded over twice as many earthquakes as California in 2014, and by August 2015 more than six times as many of magnitude 3 or more.
